items.title: Appendix A: Glossary of AI Terms for Designers
items.content:
# **Appendix A: Glossary of AI Terms for Designers**

- Agent: An AI system that takes actions in a loop (read, decide, act, check, continue) rather than just answering a single prompt.
- Agentic experience (AX): Designing for products that act on the user's behalf, where much of the work is helping people oversee and judge what the AI did.
- Algorithm: A step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or accomplishing a task.
- Bias (in AI): Systematic skew in AI outputs that disadvantages certain groups, usually inherited from skewed training data.
- Context window: How much text a model can hold in mind at once; when a session runs long, older details fall out of it and get 'forgotten.'
- Design engineer: A designer who works at the seam where design decisions become production code, often prototyping with structural continuity to the real product.
- Fine-tuning: Additional training on specific data to specialize a general-purpose model.
- Generative AI: AI that produces new content (text, images, code, audio, video) rather than only analyzing existing content.
- Grounding: Tying AI output to verified source data to reduce hallucination and keep answers traceable.
- Hallucination: When a model produces confident, plausible-sounding, but incorrect or fabricated information.
- Inference: Using a trained model to generate outputs on new inputs.
- Large Language Model (LLM): A model trained on massive text data that generates language by predicting the next chunk of text.
- MCP (Model Context Protocol): An open standard (from Anthropic, late 2024) for connecting AI tools to other tools and real context; Figma's MCP server streams live design data into coding tools like Cursor.
- Multimodal: A model that handles more than text, such as images or audio; the reason 'screenshot in, interface out' works.
- Prompt: The input you give an AI to guide its output.
- Prompt engineering: Crafting prompts (context, constraints, examples) to get better, less generic results.
- RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback): A training step that tunes models to be helpful and agreeable, and a root cause of sycophancy.
- Synthetic users: AI that role-plays a target user and answers as if it were them; useful for hypotheses, not a substitute for real research.
- Sycophancy: A model's tendency to tell you what you want to hear, agreeing with the framing of your prompt instead of pushing back.
- Token: A unit of text a model processes, roughly a word or word-fragment.
- Training data: The data a model learns from; its coverage and skew shape what the model is good and bad at.
- Transformer: The neural-network architecture underlying most modern LLMs.
- Vibe coding: Coined by Andrej Karpathy (Feb 2025); building software by describing intent and letting AI write the code with minimal review. 'Vibe design' is the interface-focused sibling.

items.title: Appendix B: Tool Landscape
items.content:
# **Appendix B: Tool Landscape (2026)**

Tools change fast. Treat this as a snapshot of categories and current examples, not a permanent ranking. Look past the logo to the capability.

## **Frontier Models**

Claude (Anthropic): Strong on analysis, long context, and clean UI generation. Often the pick for near-usable interface code.

GPT-5 (OpenAI): Capable generalist for research, ideation, writing, and code.

Gemini 3 Pro (Google): Strongest unified multimodal stack (text, image, audio, video, code) and a leader on raw web-app generation.

The practical takeaway: model choice now affects design-output quality. Run the same prompt through two before you commit.

## **Prompt-to-Prototype and Design-to-Code**

v0 (Vercel): Front-end scaffolds, landing pages, dashboards from prompts (React + Tailwind).

Lovable: Text-to-app with backend logic; suited to MVPs; integrates with Figma and GitHub.

Bolt: Fast visual previews from natural language.

Cursor: AI code editor for working inside a real codebase with context and inline debugging.

Replit: Collaborative building with hosting and deploy.

Figma Make: Prompt-to-code inside Figma (GA); edit by highlighting and describing changes.

Figma First Draft: Full low-fi screens from a text brief in seconds.

UX Pilot / Magic Patterns / Google Stitch: Wireframe-to-hi-fi generation, design-system import, and export to Figma or clean HTML/CSS.

Reality check: output is prototype-quality. A 2025 Veracode analysis found ~45% of AI-generated code samples failed security tests. Review before anything ships, especially auth and databases.

## **Image Generation**

Midjourney: High aesthetic quality for moodboards and concept art.

DALL-E (via ChatGPT) and Stable Diffusion: General-purpose and open-source/local options.

Use for mood and exploration; rebuild final designs in real tools to avoid the industry's growing sameness.

## **Research and Analysis**

Dovetail: Central qual repository with AI tagging, theming, and summarizing.

Looppanel: High-accuracy transcription, auto-tagging, searchable repository.

Notably: Transcription, clustering, sentiment, highlight reels.

Maze: Usability/concept testing at speed, plus AI-moderated interviews.

Synthetic Users: Simulated interviews. The most contested category; treat findings as hypotheses, never as real research (see Chapter 5).

## **Infrastructure**

MCP (Model Context Protocol): The standard connecting AI tools to real context. Figma's Dev Mode MCP server streams your variables and components into coding agents so output stays on-system.

items.title: Appendix C: Sample Prompts Library
items.content:
# **Appendix C: Sample Prompts Library**

Starting points, not finished prompts. Add your own context and constraints, and edit the output.

## **Research Prompts**

_'Summarize this interview transcript for these things only: the main pain points, specific feature requests, anything that surprised me, and two or three quotes that show real emotion. Note where the transcript is ambiguous rather than guessing.'_

_'Across these 10 interview summaries, what themes recur? For each, tell me how many participants raised it, not just "several," and give one example quote per theme.'_

_'Draft 12 interview questions about people's habits and frustrations with [product type]. Avoid leading questions; flag any question that assumes an answer.'_

## **Ideation Prompts**

_'Give me 5 genuinely different approaches to [problem], not variations on one idea. Here's the real situation: [context]. We can't do [constraint].'_

_'What assumptions are we making about how users complete [task]? For each, describe what we'd design differently if it were false.'_

_'How do 3 unrelated industries solve [challenge]? Give a concrete example from each and how it might transfer.'_

## **Visual and Prototype Prompts**

_'[Image tool] Moodboard for [product]: [mood], [color direction], [composition]. Generate several variations exploring the feeling from different angles.'_

_'[Prompt-to-app tool] A [screen] with [key elements]. Keep it responsive. Use our design system if imported.'_

## **UX Writing Prompts**

_'Suggest 5 labels for a button that [action]. Tone: [description]. Plain words, no filler.'_

_'Write an error message for when [situation]. Explain the problem, give the fix, don't scold. One or two sentences.'_

_'Review this copy for AI-writing tells: inflated words (leverage, seamless, robust), templates ("not just X but Y"), em-dash overuse, and both-sides hedging. Rewrite it plainly with a clear point of view.'_

## **Design-to-Code Prompts**

_'Generate HTML and CSS that replicates this screen. Use Tailwind. Make it responsive. Then list anything you were unsure about.'_

_'Generate a React + TypeScript component from these specs: [specs]. Include all states. Flag any assumption you made about data.'_

## **Review Prompts**

_'Review this design against Nielsen's 10 heuristics. For each, rate compliance and name any violation with the reason.'_

_'Evaluate this design for accessibility: contrast, text size, touch targets, screen-reader labels. Be specific about what fails.'_

items.title: Appendix D: Career Transition Checklist
items.content:
# **Appendix D: Career Transition Checklist**

Use this to prepare for AI-era UX roles. The market is sorting for judgment plus AI fluency, so weight the checklist toward decisions, not tool trivia.

## **Skills Development**

- Working proficiency with at least one frontier model (Claude, GPT, or Gemini)
- Tried at least one prompt-to-app or design-to-code tool (v0, Lovable, Figma Make, Cursor) on a real screen
- Can read enough HTML/CSS/JS to tell when generated code is wrong
- Practiced evaluation literacy: judging AI output for accuracy, fairness, and fit, not just accepting it
- Understand the failure modes: hallucination, sycophancy, homogenization, and why synthetic users aren't research
- Familiar with AI features in your primary design tools
- Comfortable with AI ethics: bias, privacy, manipulation, disclosure, and the slop problem

## **Portfolio Updates**

- At least one case study that shows how you directed AI: what you kept, what you cut, and why
- Evidence of judgment, not just polished screens
- If possible, a case study of designing an AI-powered feature (transparency, control, failure handling)
- A personal project that proves genuine interest, not box-checking

## **Interview Preparation**

- Concrete stories of using AI in real work, including a time you caught it being wrong
- A both-eyes-open point of view: powerful tool, needs direction, breaks in known ways
- Ready to discuss ethical trade-offs specifically, not in the abstract
- Can answer 'How is AI changing the designer's role?' without hype or doom
- Researched the target company's actual AI features and public positions

## **Ongoing Development**

- A standing habit: a little time each week to try new tools and form a fast, critical opinion
- Following a few worthwhile voices in AI and UX
- Sharing learnings with peers or in writing
- Keeping fundamentals sharp underneath the tools, so you stay the one who can judge the output
